title: 如何使用 Whisper 转录数千小时的音频？
author: Viswaretas Kotra
content:
Run Whisper as a sharded GPU batch job with faster-whisper's batched pipeline, and write one done marker per audio file, so a reclaimed machine repeats one file instead of the archive. Nodus runs each shard as one index of a Job on interruptible capacity and restores the done markers after a reclaim. If your GPU matches faster-whisper's published 46x real time, 10,000 hours of audio is about 217 GPU-hours: $93.48 on an L4 listed at $0.43/hr, against $2,700 on OpenAI's gpt-transcribe.

The audio part is what makes this different from batch LLM inference, which uses the same sharding idea. Files are long and uneven, some are silent or corrupt, languages vary, and the unit of work you can safely skip is a whole file, not a row.

Which Whisper model and library should you use?

For bulk transcription, use the turbo model through faster-whisper unless you need translation. OpenAI's Whisper README lists six sizes. turbo is an optimized large-v3 with 809M parameters, about 6 GB of VRAM and roughly 8x the speed of large, "with a minimal degradation in accuracy".

Model Parameters VRAM (approx.) Speed vs large
tiny 39M 1 GB ~10x
base 74M 1 GB ~7x
small 244M 2 GB ~4x
medium 769M 5 GB ~2x
large 1,550M 10 GB 1x
turbo 809M 6 GB ~8x

Source: the openai/whisper README, where relative speed was measured on English speech on an A100.


Every Whisper size fits on a 24 GB card, so pick the GPU on cost per audio hour, not memory.

Two exceptions change the choice. turbo is not trained for translation, so for non-English speech into English the README points to medium or large. The .en models tend to do better on English-only audio, mostly at the tiny and base sizes.

The library matters as much as the model. The faster-whisper README says it is up to 4 times faster than openai-whisper at the same accuracy. In its own large-v2 benchmark on an NVIDIA RTX 3070 Ti, 13 minutes of audio took 2 minutes 23 seconds with openai-whisper and 17 seconds with faster-whisper at batch_size=8 in fp16, using 6,090 MB of VRAM.

How many GPU-hours do 10,000 hours of audio take?

GPU time is audio duration divided by your real-time factor. That 17-second figure is 780 seconds of audio in 17 seconds, about 46x real time. It came from one consumer card and one 13-minute file, so treat it as a starting parameter and measure your own.

Take an archive of 10,000 hours, and an NVIDIA L4 24 GB listed at $0.43/hr on the Nodus pricing page.

  • At 46x: 10,000 / 46 = 217.4 GPU-hours, and 217.4 x $0.43 = $93.48, under a cent per audio hour.
  • At 20x: 500 GPU-hours, or $215.00.
  • At 10x: 1,000 GPU-hours, or $430.00.

The same audio is 600,000 minutes. OpenAI's pricing page lists gpt-transcribe at an estimated $0.0045 per minute, which is $2,700, and the deprecated whisper-1 model at $0.006 per minute, which is $3,600. Prices checked November 26, 2026.


At under half of faster-whisper's published speed, self-hosting still costs less than a tenth of gpt-transcribe, before engineering time.

The GPU-hour figure leaves out model loads, audio decoding on the CPU and the hours you spend building the job. Our turbo script should beat the large-v2 benchmark speed, but we have not measured it on Nodus GPUs, so the 46x stays an assumption. An RTX 4090 24 GB at $0.29/hr is worth calibrating against the L4.

How do you handle long files, silence and mixed languages?

Let the batched pipeline split each file, and fix the settings that matter for an archive. Whisper reads audio in 30-second windows, as the openai-whisper README describes. The faster-whisper BatchedInferencePipeline turns on voice activity detection (VAD) by default, cuts speech into chunks of at most 30 seconds and decodes up to batch_size chunks at once, per its transcribe.py.

That means you never cut audio files yourself. VAD also skips long silences, so a two-hour recording with forty minutes of speech costs roughly forty minutes of decoding.

Language detection needs a decision. The batched pipeline detects language from one segment by default (language_detection_segments=1). If your archive is known to be one language, pass language="en" and skip detection. If it is mixed, keep language_probability in every record and send low-confidence files to a second pass.

Ask for word timestamps up front. word_timestamps=True adds per-word start and end times, which subtitles, search and alignment all need, and a rerun to add them costs the whole job again. Store one JSON record per file with segments, words and the detected language, and render SRT from that.

How do you make the job survive preemption?

Make the audio file the unit of work, and record each finished file in the checkpoint directory. Interruptible capacity can be reclaimed, and how often that happens depends on the GPU and region. A shard that restarts from zero gives the savings back.

The script below follows four rules:

  1. A manifest lists every file with an ID and its duration in seconds.
  2. Files are split by duration, longest first, each to the least-loaded shard, so shards finish together and the split is identical on every attempt.
  3. Each finished file becomes a done marker written to a temp file and renamed, so a marker is complete or absent.
  4. Missing or corrupt files get a failed marker and are skipped; any other error stops the run.

It reads NODUS_INDEX, NODUS_COMPLETIONS, NODUS_CHECKPOINT_DIR and NODUS_OUTPUTS_DIR, which every Nodus Job sees, per the Jobs guide. 

import json, os
from pathlib import Path
import av
from faster_whisper import WhisperModel, BatchedInferencePipeline, decode_audio

INDEX = int(os.environ["NODUS_INDEX"])
SHARDS = int(os.environ["NODUS_COMPLETIONS"])
STATE = Path(os.environ["NODUS_CHECKPOINT_DIR"])
OUT = Path(os.environ["NODUS_OUTPUTS_DIR"]) / "transcripts"
AUDIO = Path("/data/audio")

def my_files(manifest):
    # Longest file first, always to the least-loaded shard: the same split on every attempt.
    load, mine = [0.0] * SHARDS, []
    for r in sorted(manifest, key=lambda r: (-r["seconds"], r["id"])):
        s = min(range(SHARDS), key=lambda i: (load[i], i))
        load[s] += r["seconds"]
        if s == INDEX:
            mine.append(r)
    return mine

def srt(segments):
    def ts(t):
        ms = round(t * 1000)
        return f"{ms // 3600000:02}:{ms // 60000 % 60:02}:{ms // 1000 % 60:02},{ms % 1000:03}"
    return "".join(f"{i}\n{ts(s['start'])} --> {ts(s['end'])}\n{s['text'].strip()}\n\n"
                   for i, s in enumerate(segments, 1))

manifest = [json.loads(line) for line in open(AUDIO / "manifest.jsonl")]
done_dir, fail_dir = STATE / "done", STATE / "failed"
done_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
fail_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

model = WhisperModel("turbo", device="cuda", compute_type="float16")
pipe = BatchedInferencePipeline(model=model)

for r in my_files(manifest):
    done = done_dir / f"{r['id']}.json"
    if done.exists() or (fail_dir / f"{r['id']}.txt").exists():
        continue  # finished (or recorded as bad) by an earlier attempt
    try:
        audio = decode_audio(str(AUDIO / r["path"]))  # 16 kHz mono float32
    except (OSError, av.error.FFmpegError) as e:  # missing or corrupt file only
        (fail_dir / f"{r['id']}.txt").write_text(repr(e))
        continue
    segments, info = pipe.transcribe(audio, batch_size=16, word_timestamps=True)
    segs = [{"start": s.start, "end": s.end, "text": s.text,
             "words": [{"start": w.start, "end": w.end, "word": w.word} for w in s.words]}
            for s in segments]  # transcription runs here
    rec = {"id": r["id"], "language": info.language,
           "language_probability": info.language_probability, "segments": segs}
    tmp = done.with_suffix(".tmp")
    tmp.write_text(json.dumps(rec))
    os.replace(tmp, done)  # a done marker is either complete or absent

(OUT / "srt").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with open(OUT / f"part-{INDEX}.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for p in sorted(done_dir.glob("*.json")):
        rec = json.loads(p.read_text())
        f.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")
        (OUT / "srt" / f"{rec['id']}.srt").write_text(srt(rec["segments"]))
failed = sorted(p.stem for p in fail_dir.glob("*.txt"))
(OUT / f"failed-{INDEX}.txt").write_text("\n".join(failed))

We tested it on a CPU in two ways. First, with the real tiny.en model on three LibriSpeech clips plus one missing file: three transcripts with word timestamps and valid SRT, one failed marker, and a rerun that skipped everything. Second, with the transcriber replaced by a stub: 200 files in 4 shards, two of them missing, each process killed after 20 files and restarted. The restarts transcribed only the remaining files, every file was transcribed exactly once, and the shards each held 47.3 to 47.4 hours of audio.

The narrow except comes from a failure we hit. Our first version caught every exception, and with faster-whisper 1.2.1 and PyAV 19.0.2 every file failed with TypeError: open() got an unexpected keyword argument 'metadata_errors'. A broad catch would have marked the whole archive as bad files and exited cleanly.

Pinning PyAV 15.1.0 fixed it, and an environment error now stops the run instead of hiding. Pin both versions in your image.

How do you run the shards on Nodus?

Upload the audio and manifest to a Volume, then submit the script as an Indexed Job on interruptible capacity. Every flag below is from the nodus run CLI reference. The image needs faster-whisper with CUDA 12 and cuDNN 9, which its README notes are in nvidia/cuda:12.3.2-cudnn9-runtime-ubuntu22.04. 

nodus run --name transcribe-archive --gpu L4 --image YOUR_WHISPER_IMAGE \
  --completions 8 --parallelism 8 --interruptible --profile Cost \
  --volume audio:/data/audio:ro --max-cost 120 --dry-run \
  --output transcripts=/nodus/outputs/transcripts -- python transcribe.py

--dry-run prints the expected cost before anything runs, so review it, then drop the flag. --interruptible with no value means prefer.

Checkpointed is the default recovery mode, so after a reclaim the new attempt starts with /nodus/state restored and skips every file it finds there. On a reclaim notice, Nodus also asks for an urgent checkpoint before the old machine goes away, per attempts and recovery. --max-cost is a hard cap: at $120 the Job saves its state and suspends rather than spending more.

The split decides what a reclaim costs. Using the 46x example on an L4 at $0.43/hr:

Setup Work at risk per reclaim Cost
One run, nothing saved Up to 217.4 GPU-hours Up to $93.48
8 shards, restart the shard Up to 27.2 GPU-hours Up to $11.68
8 shards, per-file markers One file in flight, 78 seconds for a 1-hour file Under $0.01

A file that is mid-transcription when the machine goes is transcribed again, which is why very long recordings are worth keeping under a few hours each.

When is a hosted transcription API the better choice?

Use the API when the job is small, one-off or needs a model you cannot run. At $0.0045 per minute, 100 hours of audio costs $27 on gpt-transcribe, less than the engineering time to build an image and calibrate speed. OpenAI also says its GPT-4o transcription models improve word error rate over the original Whisper models, so the API can win on accuracy too.

Our decision rule, from the numbers above:

  1. Under a few hundred hours, or a one-off: use the API.
  2. Thousands of hours, recurring archives, or audio that must stay on hardware you control: self-host.
  3. Before committing, run one hour of your own audio through turbo on an L4 and an RTX 4090, and through the API. Compare word error on a hand-checked sample and cost per audio hour, and keep the cheapest option that passes.
  4. Need English translation of other languages: use multilingual large-v3 or medium, not turbo.

FAQ

Does Whisper do speaker diarization?

No. Whisper outputs text and timestamps, not speakers. The faster-whisper README lists community projects such as WhisperX that add diarization on top of it.

Do I need FFmpeg in the image?

Not for faster-whisper, which decodes audio with PyAV and its bundled FFmpeg libraries. openai-whisper does need the ffmpeg command-line tool installed.

Can Whisper invent text that was not said?

Yes. OpenAI's model card warns about hallucinations and repetitive text, likely worse in low-resource languages. Spot-check a sample of transcripts, especially in low-resource languages, before you rely on them.

Can I see the cost per audio file on Nodus?

Yes, if your script calls nodus.log.unit(id, ms) after each file. The Job's Work outcomes view then shows completed units, median and p95 time per unit, and cost per reported unit.

Is CPU transcription an option?

For small models, yes. In the faster-whisper README, the small model in int8 at batch_size=8 transcribed the 13-minute file in 51 seconds on 8 threads of an Intel Core i7-12700K. Larger models are where the GPU earns its cost.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.
aiSummary: 本文介绍了一套实用方案，讲解如何借助 Whisper 转录数千小时的音频，并采用 GPU 分片、成本优化和容错检查点策略。
oneSentenceSummary: 本文介绍了一套实用方案，讲解如何借助 Whisper 转录数千小时的音频，并采用 GPU 分片、成本优化和容错检查点策略。
summary: 本文详细介绍了一种可扩展的方案：使用 OpenAI 的 Whisper 模型和 faster-whisper 库，通过 GPU 分片批处理任务转录海量音频档案。文章建议对英语音频使用 turbo 模型（809M 参数、6GB VRAM、速度约为实时的 46 倍），并计算了转录成本：使用 L4 GPU 自托管转录 10，000 小时音频的费用为 $93.48，而通过 OpenAI API 则为 $2，700。该方案通过带 VAD 的批量推理跳过静音，处理长文件和多语言混合音频，并使用 done/failed 标记实现基于检查点的恢复，以应对 GPU 抢占。文章还通过 Python 脚本展示了分片策略，并根据任务量和控制需求比较了自托管与托管 API 的适用场景。

mainPoints.point: 使用 faster-whisper 的 turbo 模型并进行 GPU 分片，以低成本批量转录音频
mainPoints.explanation: turbo 模型的速度是 large 模型的 8 倍，准确率损失极小。在 L4 GPU 上转录 10，000 小时音频约需 217 GPU 小时，费用为 $93.48；通过 OpenAI API 则需 $2，700。

mainPoints.point: 使用 done/failed 标记实现基于检查点的恢复，提升容错能力
mainPoints.explanation: 每完成一个文件，就以原子方式写入 done 标记。这样即使任务中断，也能恢复运行并跳过已处理的文件，将每次重新抢占造成的成本从 $93.48 降至 $0.01 以下。

mainPoints.point: 使用启用 VAD 的批量处理流水线，自动处理静音并切分长音频
mainPoints.explanation: BatchedInferencePipeline 会执行语音活动检测，将语音切分为 30 秒的片段并跳过静音，因此无需手动预处理音频。

keyQuotes: 如果你的 GPU 能达到 faster-whisper 公布的实时速度 46 倍，那么转录 10，000 小时音频约需 217 GPU 小时：按每小时 $0.43 计算，使用 L4 的费用为 $93.48，而使用 OpenAI 的 gpt-transcribe 则需 $2，700。
如果机器在转录过程中宕机，正在处理的文件就得重新转录。因此，超长录音最好控制在几小时以内。
如果任务量小、只需处理一次，或者需要使用你无法自行运行的模型，就使用 API。按每分钟 $0.0045 计算，100 小时音频使用 gpt-transcribe 的费用为 $27，低于构建镜像并校准速度所需的工程成本。
